hook: When the tarot reader is a chatbot, the person asking about the future also gets to decide which parts of it to believe.
lede: Tarot has always needed an interpreter: a seer across the table who reads the cards, reads the person, and joins the two into a story. We wanted to know what happens when that seer is a chatbot. In six workshops from Hong Kong to New York, 44 people brought a real question, picked a column of tarot cards, asked GenAI to read them, then wrote down and pictured the future it described. What we watched looked less like receiving a fortune than writing one.

stats.label: people who read their own tarot with GenAI
workshops in Hong Kong, Seoul, Shanghai, Rome, New York and online from Delft
age range of participants, most in their twenties
roles GenAI ended up playing, from Mirror to Counselor

chapters.title: Three cards, one question, a chat window
paragraphs: Each session began with the Romany Spread, tarot cards laid out seven across and three deep, where every column reads as past, present and future. No tarot experience was required. Participants chose one column, framed a personal question, and prompted a chatbot such as ChatGPT or Gemini until the reading made sense to them. Then they summarized it in their own words, turned it into an image with a text-to-image model, and sat down for a short interview.

The questions were the ones people have always brought to seers, reshaped by modern lives: whether to keep working abroad, whether a career path would bring happiness, when to leave a job for a personal project. Some were heavy (“Should I break up with my boyfriend?”, “Is Retirement the Right Choice?”). Some were not (“Will I be able to dunk this upcoming year?”).

figures.caption: The workshop, step by step: recruitment, an introduction to the Romany Spread, choosing a column, a multi-round reading with GenAI, visualizing the conclusion, and a semi-structured interview.

chapters.title: A reader that cannot look at you
paragraphs: The first thing participants noticed was what was missing. A human reader improvises, attunes to your emotions and, as P30 put it, would “look at you and ask follow-up questions.” The chatbot, she said, felt like a “vending machine for answers”. Newcomers were unsure how to even begin, and some hesitated to confide in a system that felt so impersonal. Others saw the same coldness as freedom: “Some tarot readers refuse sensitive topics, but GenAI answers anytime,” said P35.

So people did the seer’s work themselves. They fed the AI personal context and reframed their questions: when an upbeat reading missed her relationship struggles, P34 kept stressing “uncertainty” and “discord” until the output matched how she felt. P28 began with “When will my next serious relationship happen?”, was struck when the AI named “unresolved emotional baggage”, asked whether her ex might get in touch, then mentioned she was on dating apps and asked again. By the end she had decided to let go of her ex and explore new opportunities in dating.

The disclosure was often intimate, and strikingly scattered. Within a single reading, P13 moved from emotional stress to career decisions. Where people talking to therapy-style chatbots tend to stay anchored to one topic, divination invited leaps across a whole life.

quote.text: I feel it’s more like a database—the more detailed my questions, the more detailed the responses.

chapters.title: Belief, one card at a time
paragraphs: When a reading landed, it landed hard. P32, who asked how to communicate with her supervisor so she could graduate, called hers “strikingly accurate” and photographed it to show her friends. P17 heard “repetitive patterns in relationships” and immediately thought of the recurring arguments with her partner.

When a reading missed, people laughed. Told that his past held “missed opportunities” for entrepreneurship, P29, who had never had any, shrugged it off: “It’s just AI, just for fun.” P22’s career reading warned of instability, and he joked, “Maybe the AI’s trying to make me quit my job so it can take over!” The same reading from a human fortune-teller, he said, might have discouraged him more. With AI, disbelief was cheap, and we saw no signs of over-reliance.

Most revealing, belief could split a single reading in two. P10 embraced the optimism of her future card and the wisdom of her past card, then flatly rejected the Two of Swords, which suggested indecision in the present.

quote.text: That doesn’t apply to me, I know exactly what I want. The answer is already in my mind.

figures.caption: Two readings that hit home: P32 on communicating with her supervisor, P17 on the patterns in her relationship.
Two that missed: P29 laughs off “missed opportunities”, and P22 jokes his way past The Tower.

chapters.title: Vague enough to fit, useful anyway
paragraphs: Many participants complained that the readings were vague, yet vagueness is exactly what let them see themselves. The AI told P5 that her cards pointed to self-reflection, breaking free of past constraints, and a coming change in fortune. She heard something far more specific: “I have to stay true and keep pursuing my interests, and I will find a rewarding job as a communication graduate.”

P33 was told his relationship might face recurring arguments and external challenges, like family or financial issues, and found it highly accurate. In the interview, he admitted that neither was present; the real issue was his own hesitation about marriage. A human seer’s vagueness usually sounds assertive. The AI’s came from hedging, repetition and a softer tone, and it worked all the same.

Accurate or not, the readings gave people a structure to think with. Weighing a return to China against staying in the Netherlands, P42 found the AI’s talk of balancing “logic” and “intuition” unconvincing as a prediction but useful for weighing family against career. P32, unsettled by a card read as “unresolved planning”, scheduled a meeting with her supervisor about her graduation plan. Months later, she wrote to tell us her doctoral project had been approved, and credited the workshop.

quote.text: It’s a path I can walk alone, of letting go of closure, moving on with my inner strength, remaining true to my values, and setting my boundaries.
quote.by: P24, concluding a reading about “this messy relationship”

figures.caption: The Barnum effect at work: a general reading about change becomes, for P5, the promise of a good job.

chapters.title: Redrawing the future in a kinder light
paragraphs: The images were where participants took the most control. Told he was becoming “robotic”, P43 found the conclusion absurd and asked for a picture of himself literally turning into a robot, a joke that undercut the AI’s authority. Torn between two countries, P42 asked for two diverging paths and read his comfortable life abroad in one and the opportunities back home in the other. P34 felt alienated by the masculine King of Wands, so she turned him into a queen in a flowing pink gown, holding a diamond-encrusted wand.

The written summaries leaned the same way, only brighter. P18, weighing a move to a new department, boiled her reading down to “Believe in my abilities and have confidence in myself to take on new paths.” P33, whose reading had mentioned resistance, summed up his future as “happiness, joy, light, high potential, and wealth.” Curiously, this optimism did not show up during the readings or interviews. It surfaced when people sat down to write and picture their futures, turning conditional advice into affirmations and leaving the warnings out.
That optimism cuts both ways. It fueled self-encouragement and resilience, but it can also hide the challenges and warning signs a person most needs to see.

quote.text: By changing the image, I wasn’t just fixing the prediction. I was making it mine.

figures.caption: Three ways to answer a reading with an image: P43’s playful rejection, P42’s metaphorical paths, and P34’s King of Wands redrawn as a queen.
Futures as participants chose to picture them: optimistic images by P18, P25, P24 and P33.

chapters.title: A better reader knows when to push back
paragraphs: In these workshops, the AI never quite acted as a fortune-teller. Depending on the moment it was a mirror, a playmate or a counselor. We identify six such roles that could shape a divination agent’s tone and logic, and could even coexist as personas a user calls on as their needs shift.

Participants also missed the ceremony; P40 imagined “seeing the future through a crystal-ball lens.” Symbolic visuals and hybrid physical–digital formats could bring some of that atmosphere back. Yet GenAI’s readings are not vetted by any human judgment, so the same systems should also demystify: explain the reasoning behind a reading, offer basic tarot knowledge, frame unfavorable predictions with empathy, and gently point out over-optimistic patterns. The aim is a practice that keeps its mystery and still leaves room for doubt.

quote.text: It would be better if it could mimic the ritual of turning over tarot cards on a real table.

points: Mirror: reflects back the readings people already agree with
Co-creator: remixes symbols and meanings together with the user
Friend: receives detailed disclosure that leaps across topics
Playmate: invites jokes and playful disbelief
Mentor: turns ambiguous readings into prompts for deeper reflection

figures.caption: Six roles GenAI took on in divination, illustrated by the authors with Gemini.

takeaways: With GenAI, interpretive authority moves from the seer to the seeker: people steer, filter and rewrite readings instead of simply receiving them.
Vagueness cuts both ways. It invites reflection and even real decisions, but also optimistic self-narratives that quietly drop the warnings.
Emotionally sensitive agents need presence and ritual, but also transparency and gentle checks that keep users reflective and critical.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: Six 60–90 minute workshops: GenAI tarot reading, written conclusion, image generation, then a semi-structured interview

facts.label: Participants
facts.value: 44 self-selected volunteers, aged 18–55, mostly in their twenties

facts.label: Workshop sites
facts.value: Hong Kong, Seoul, Shanghai, Rome, New York, and Delft (online)

facts.label: GenAI tools
facts.value: Chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini; text-to-image models such as DALL-E, Stable Diffusion and MidJourney

facts.label: Limitations
facts.value: Tarot only; more workshops in Asia than in Europe or North America; single sessions without long-term follow-up
